core: working definition (WHO-attributed): hand hygiene is a general term referring to any action of hand cleansing — with soap and water or an alcohol-based hand sanitizer

method rule (CDC): soap and water when hands are visibly dirty or greasy or soiled with blood/body fluids; otherwise an alcohol-based sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol, recommended whenever soap and water are not readily available

handwashing technique (CDC): wet with clean running water, apply soap, lather backs of hands / between fingers / under nails, scrub at least 20 seconds, rinse, dry with clean towel or air dryer; sanitizer: rub every surface until dry
the WHO's My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene framework, all five moments named verbatim with a one-line reason each
gloves do not replace hand hygiene — required before donning and after removal (WHO)

why it works: breaks the hands-as-route link in transmission (CDC 2002 mechanism: patient skin/surfaces -> caregiver hands -> next patient); failure to perform hand hygiene is the leading cause of health-care-associated infections (CDC 2002)
honest framing: hand hygiene is the cheapest life-saving technology in health care; WHO improvement programmes can prevent up to 50% of avoidable infections and return ~16x their cost
supporting: CDC consumer page (About Handwashing) lists routine hand-hygiene moments (before preparing food, after using the toilet, etc.) and describes handwashing with soap as one of the best ways to stay healthy

MedlinePlus corroborates: germs are microorganisms (bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites) spread by touch, coughs, contaminated surfaces; wash hands at least 20 seconds; hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol
WHO 2009 guidelines: hand hygiene is the most important measure to protect patients, healthcare workers, and the environment from microbial contamination; five moments with full rationale
WHO Five Moments poster (2021) confirms the moment names and their placement in the flow of care

standard precautions as a whole and PPE selection (owned by nursing-and-allied-health-foundations:foundations:standard-precautions)
transmission-based precautions — contact, droplet, airborne (owned by nursing-and-allied-health-foundations:foundations:transmission-based-precautions)

claims.claim: The WHO defines hand hygiene as a general term referring to any action of hand cleansing — with soap and water or an alcohol-based hand rub/sanitizer.

The CDC rule for method choice: wash with soap and water when hands are visibly dirty or greasy or soiled with blood or body fluids; otherwise an alcohol-based hand sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol is effective, and the CDC recommends it whenever soap and water are not readily available.

The CDC's handwashing technique: wet hands with clean running water, apply soap, lather the backs of the hands, between the fingers, and under the nails, scrub for at least 20 seconds, rinse, and dry with a clean towel or air dryer; for sanitizer, rub the product over every hand surface until dry.

The WHO's My 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene framework names the five moments health-care workers must clean their hands during patient care: 1) before touching a patient, 2) before a clean or aseptic procedure, 3) after body fluid exposure risk, 4) after touching a patient, 5) after touching patient surroundings.
Gloves do not replace hand hygiene: hand hygiene is required before putting on gloves and again after removing them, because gloves protect but do not clean.

Failure to perform appropriate hand hygiene is considered the leading cause of health-care-associated infections and the spread of multiresistant organisms (CDC 2002); the WHO describes hand hygiene as the most important measure for protecting patients, healthcare workers, and the environment from microbial contamination.

The transmission mechanism hand hygiene interrupts: germs on a patient's skin or on nearby objects are transferred to a caregiver's hands, survive there, and travel to the next patient when the hands are not cleaned at the right moments.

Hand-hygiene improvement programmes can prevent up to 50% of avoidable infections acquired during health-care delivery and generate economic savings on average 16 times the cost of implementation (WHO) — the 'cheapest life-saving technology' framing.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Which method is 'better' — handwashing or hand sanitizer
positions: CDC and WHO present alcohol-based hand rub as the preferred routine method for hand hygiene in health care when hands are not visibly dirty (better efficacy against most germs, faster, better compliance)

Soap and water is required when hands are visibly dirty or greasy or soiled with blood/body fluids, and preferred after certain exposures (e.g. spore-forming organisms), because sanitizer can be blocked by dirt
MedlinePlus presents both as valid everyday options with the same 60%-alcohol threshold
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the method-selection rule (visible dirt or body fluids -> soap and water; otherwise sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol or handwashing both work) instead of declaring one method superior overall.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The recommended duration of hand cleaning varies slightly across sources
positions: CDC consumer guidance: scrub with soap and water for at least 20 seconds
WHO 2009 guidelines recommend rubbing with alcohol-based products for 20-30 seconds
MedlinePlus: wash hands for at least 20 seconds (about the time to hum 'Happy Birthday' twice)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the CDC's at-least-20-seconds figure as the routine standard and describes the rub-until-dry technique for sanitizer without asserting a conflicting second count.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Naming and numbering of the five moments in different WHO materials
positions: WHO 2009 guidelines name Moment 2 'before an aseptic task' in some passages and 'before a clean/aseptic procedure' in the five-moments materials
The My 5 Moments poster (2021) uses 'before a clean/aseptic procedure' with the same numbering 1-5
Some national guidance reorders or renames moments (e.g. 'before aseptic tasks' as a separate category)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the five moment names verbatim from the WHO five-moments materials and the 2009 guidelines, which agree on the framework and numbering.

rightsIssues: CDC and MedlinePlus are U.S. government works (public domain, attributed); WHO sources are reference-only — no source wording reproduced; all prose is original synthesis and all examples are original.
